extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of ancient Greek philosophy and humor theory; readers interested in philosophical analyses of laughter
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Plato's criteria for what makes a person or situation 'ridiculous' as set out in Philebus (48–50) and related Republic passages. Focuses on conditions on the target, audience, affective structure, and normative warnings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-ignorance (agnoia heautou)
rubrics_metrics.description: The target imagines themself to be wealthier, more beautiful, or more virtuous than they really are; a delusion of self is required for genuine ridiculousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without this delusion of self the target is not ridiculous but pitiable. Emphasize the contrast between the target's self-image and objective reality when applying this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powerlessness of the target
rubrics_metrics.description: The self-deceived person must be too weak to retaliate; if the target is dangerous or able to strike back they are feared rather than laughed at.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A self-deceived tyrant is an example of non-ridiculousness: strength or ability to harm removes comic status. Only a harmless fool elicits comic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party spectator (external perspective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter occurs from a spectator outside the target, who compares the target's self-image to reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ridicule requires an external comparative judgment; self-directed irony or shared awareness undermines this condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed-pleasure affective structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic enjoyment is a mixed state combining pleasure (from perceiving the target's self-ignorance) and pain (envy/malice/epichairekakia); the two are intertwined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating humor, identify both the pleasurable recognition and the element of delight in another's misfortune; Plato treats the blend as constitutive of the comic feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral suspectness of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Because laughter involves a malicious component, it is morally questionable; 'pure' laughter without malice is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the ethical implications of enjoyment: if the laugh depends on taking pleasure in another's harm or folly, Plato regards it as morally problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-awareness negates ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who knows and admits their own ignorance (the Socratic figure) is not ridiculous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-knowledge or explicit admission of fault removes the ironic gap between self-image and reality that generates laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger/powerfulness negates ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: If the self-deceived person is strong or dangerous, their self-deception does not produce laughter but fear or contempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether something is comic, check the balance of power; perceived ability to retaliate or harm precludes comic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure misfortune without self-deception is tragic, not comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Misfortune that does not involve self-deception does not count as ridiculous; it belongs to tragedy rather than comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between suffering that results from ignorance (comic) and suffering that is simply unfortunate (tragic). The presence of self-deception is decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience comparative stance
rubrics_metrics.description: The spectator must judge themselves to be not in the same condition as the target — a comparative judgment that separates spectator from subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy requires the audience to see themselves as superior or at least differently placed; anonymity or identification with the target reduces laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience willingness to entertain malice
rubrics_metrics.description: The spectator must be willing to entertain a slightly malicious feeling (a readiness for epichairekakia / Schadenfreude).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the audience's affective readiness: humor that depends on moral squeamishness or refusal to feel any malice will fail to produce the comic reaction Plato describes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Republic normative warning about violent laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Violent laughter destabilizes the soul, undermines dignity (especially of guardians), and should be excluded from the education of rulers; comic poets should be tightly controlled in the ideal state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a normative constraint when evaluating the appropriateness of humor in political or educational contexts: laughter that is violent or destabilizing is censurable according to Platonic ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic checklist for ridiculousness
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of diagnostic questions to determine if a joke/target is ridiculous: Does the joke target someone who falsely overestimates themselves? Is the target effectively powerless? Does the laugh require us to enjoy something morally bad? Would the joke survive if the target became aware of their own flaw?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these four quick questions as a practical test when analyzing particular jokes, scenes, or comic targets to see if they meet Plato's conditions for the ridiculous.
